This study examines the utility of mathematical models in predicting the course of SARS-CoV-2 outbreaks and their role in developing public health strategies. Unlike research papers that present models and data, this viewpoint paper reviews the strengths and limitations of various mathematical frameworks used to model infectious diseases, drawing on the author's prior work tagging models with their mathematical structure. A novel model, featuring time-dependent parameters and hospitalization categories, was also developed to assess the accuracy of existing models and their applicability to pandemic data. The results show that models based on ordinary differential equations and compartmental structures often fit SARS-CoV-2 data well but frequently exaggerate the rate of transmission and formation of herd immunity, whereas models using vulnerable populations as a category more accurately predict pandemic outcomes. The research findings highlight the importance of selecting models based on the nature of available data and the research question at hand when analysing infectious disease outbreaks, failing which, models may produce misleading outcomes. This viewpoint paper is intended to guide researchers and health authorities in choosing appropriate mathematical models to analyse SARS-CoV-2 data and develop effective public health policies. Multiple approaches have been proposed for state reconstruction, including classical tomography, which can determine the state by measuring specific non-commuting operators. Research on the dynamics of coupled optical fields has shown that initially entangled states can evolve into synchronized or even non-synchronized states, depending on their type and the interactions occurring between the fields. To better understand these processes and their outcomes, a set of non-commuting operators, including the pair-density matrix operators $-\Delta_{y}$, $-\Delta_{x}$, and the entanglement monotones $E_{M}$, $E_{N}$ were used to create a distinguishable picture of the state's dynamics in one-dimensional non-degenerate parametric oscillators. Moreover, this toolkit has applications extending beyond the realm of optics, potentially contributing to our understanding of other areas of quantum physics, including superconducting circuits and ultracold atoms.
